_comment: THE AUTHORED WALKING ORDER. This is the one piece of pure judgement in the project and it was done by hand, on a map, in one sitting. Every one of the ten routes is this sequence with the stops of the two unchosen topics removed, which is why a route never doubles back on itself for no reason and why the same two stops always fall in the same order relative to each other. pipeline/author_routes.py turns this into content/routes.json, which is what the baker actually reads.
_shape: The walk starts at the Tower, which is a dead end in the south-east and therefore has to be the start rather than a stop in the middle. It runs north to Aldgate, west along the old Roman line through Leadenhall and Cornhill, drops south to the Monument and the river, comes back up Cannon Street, crosses the City to Guildhall and St Paul's, climbs north into Smithfield and up the Fleet valley to Clerkenwell, comes back down the valley through Holborn, then runs the length of Fleet Street from east to west and finishes on the Embankment at the river.
_why_it_survives_subsetting: Removing twelve stops from a good order leaves gaps, and a gap is what makes a walk sag. The sequence was arranged so that no two consecutive stops of the SAME topic are far apart, because those are the pairs that stay adjacent when the other two topics are removed. That is the constraint that actually matters, and it is not obvious until a route fails.
_overrides_comment: A route whose key appears here keeps the order given rather than inheriting from the master sequence. Nothing needs one yet. This exists so that a single awkward combination can be fixed by hand without disturbing the other nine.
